rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The poem at a glance "who are you, little i" (1961) by E. E. Cummings is eight lines long and looks almost carelessly written — no capitals where they should be, line breaks in odd places — and is in fact built as carefully as a watch. The speaker, waking near the end of November, watches a small child ("little i") at a window, gazing out at frost and falling snow.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
The speaker addresses a small child (himself) — innocence vs adult compromise.
Unusual typography and lowercase style are part of the meaning; mention modernist technique.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: November sunset imagery: 'gold red' sky, 'the quivering leaf' — connect one image to the mood of quiet wonder.  ·  ## The themes worth an essay **Wonder as a way of seeing** — the child does not see more than the adult; the child *notices* more. **The sacredness of the ordinary moment** — frost and snow, the plainest winter props, treated as revelation. **The inner child** — the adult speaker recovering his own eyes through the child at the window.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## The title, defended "who are you, little i" is the poem's own first line, asked in the poem's own grammar — small letters included. The defence: the title is a question the poem never fully answers on purpose; it hands the reader the mystery in miniature (even the title's *i* is lower case) and lets the eight lines deepen it rather than close it. A title that asks is rarer and more honest than a title that tells.  ·  ## How NEB asks it **"Who is 'little i' in the poem?" (2–4 marks)** — hold the ambiguity: the child at the window, and the speaker's own childhood self; the poem means both. **"Why does Cummings write in lower case?"** — intimacy and smallness: the self humbled, wonder enlarged; form performing meaning.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. Who is 'little i' and what is he doing? (2 marks) — a small child gazing at the November sunset from a window.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Q. Who is 'little i' and what is he doing? (2 marks) — a small child gazing at the November sunset from a window.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## Reading it closely, line by line The opening question names the mystery before explaining it: "who are you, little i". The letter *i* — the self, reduced to its smallest possible size — is addressed as *you*, as if the speaker meets himself and is not sure which of him is speaking.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Ambiguity** — the master device: "little i" is child, past self, and letter, all at once; the poem lives on the overlap. - **Personification of a letter** — the *i* addressed as a person: typography turned into character. - **Imagery (sensory list)** — "tasting touching hearing seeing breathing": the whole body made an instrument of attention.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: The speaker watches a small child ('little i') watching the sunset — the poem is about wonder and the adult's lost ability to see freshly; state this reversal.  ·  Trick 2: Cummings's typography: lowercase 'i', broken syntax, compressed lines — the form itself enacts childlike simplicity; name the style.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. Why does Cummings write 'i' in lowercase? (1 mark) — to humble the ego and mirror the child's smallness and wonder.
